segments.text: We know AI can help us write code in seconds, and we know it can hallucinate bad information.
But between the utopian promises and the doomsday warnings, what outcomes are we completely missing?
To see why that's a hard question, we need to rewind a bit and look at a city that paid people to catch rats.
In 1902, Hanoi had a massive problem.
The brand-new sewer system became a breeding ground, and thousands of rats were swarming the streets.
The colonial government devised a plan that seemed perfectly logical.
They offered a cash bounty.
Citizens simply had to turn in a severed rat tail to collect a payment.
At first, the policy worked exactly as designed.
Tails poured into the government offices by the thousands.
The authorities patted themselves on the back, confident they had solved the infestation.
On paper, the math made sense.
The city assumed that one tail equaled one dead rat.
They tied their goal to a metric that was incredibly easy to count.
But then, residents started noticing something very strange.
Rats were still running all over the city.
They just didn't have any tails.
The rat hunters had figured out a better way to maximize their profits.
Since a rat can live a perfectly normal life without its tail, hunters simply clipped them off and let the animals go so they could keep reading.
It was simple economics.
A dead rat pays once.
A live rat pays forever.
Some of the more ambitious entrepreneurs took this logic to its absolute limit.
Instead of hunting in the sewers, they set up dedicated rat farms to ensure a steady, reliable supply of tails.
When the government finally caught on and ended the program, they were left with a mountain of severed tails.
And a city overrun by significantly more rats than when they started.
The plan failed because it ignored human adaptation.
A system built to eradicate a pest gave citizens a massive financial incentive to cultivate it.
We see this gap between intent and outcome over and over in history.
If we look at past innovations, there is a consistent disconnect between what people expected to happen and what actually did.
This infographic tracks historical gaps.
On the top left, in 1995, critics doubted e-commerce could compete with physical moles.
Today, buying online is an everyday habit.
On the top right, in 1940, experts predicted we'd commute in flying cars by now.
Yet, decades later, we still travel by road.
That flying car prediction actually came from Henry Ford.
Even the man who pioneered mass auto manufacturing couldn't accurately forecast how human transportation would evolve.
Forecast often fall flat because they project clean, ideal scenarios.
They miss the messy, stubborn, practical ways that ordinary people adapt to new tools.
Returning to our chart, the bottom left panel shows the trajectory of text messaging.
SMS was originally built just to send short technical alerts over mobile networks.
The creators never expected it to take off.
But young people adopted it and turned texting into a global standard for communication.
And this disconnect isn't limited to technology.
In Australia, the government imported cane toads specifically to eat the beetles that were destroying their sugar cane crops.
As the bottom right of our graphic shows, the toads barely controlled the beetles.
Instead, they poisoned native animals and spread uncontrollably across the entire country.
Whether you introduce a digital communications network or a biological agent,
the inventor's original intent rarely dictates the outcome.
The final result is defined by uncontrollable downstream ripple effects.
Which brings us right back to artificial intelligence.
If the optimists are forecasting a utopia and the warriors are preparing for a collapse,
what everyday realities are both camps totally blind to?
The most important thing artificial intelligence does in your entire lifetime won't be something we can map out today.
It will likely be a use case that no lab researcher or industry critic has even thought of yet.
Accepting that blind spot shouldn't make you afraid of the future.
It means you get to walk into it with your eyes open, watching the story unfold in real time.
You do not need to predict the exact destination.
You just need to recognize the uncertainty, pay close attention to what ordinary people actually do with the tech,
and build versatile skills that hold their value even when the forecast changes.
As this tech spanner reminds us, some of the biggest results are the ones nobody predicted.
And that's the best reason to stay curious.
